match.reason: No bank point teaches the average value of a function as the integral over [a, b] divided by (b − a); the closest cards cover expected value, the secant gradient (average rate of change), and cumulative distribution functions, which are different ideas.

draft.title: Average value of a function
card: The average value of f(x) on the interval [a, b] is the height of a rectangle on [a, b] that has the same area as the area under the curve.
Average value = 1/(b − a) × the integral of f(x) from a to b. The integral gives the area, and dividing by the width b − a gives the height.
Worked example: find the average value of f(x) = x² on [0, 3]. The integral of x² from 0 to 3 is [x³/3] from 0 to 3 = 9 − 0 = 9.
Divide by the width: 3 − 0 = 3. The average value is 9 ÷ 3 = 3.
draft.remember: Average value = the area under the curve divided by the width of the interval.

a.q: The integral of f(x) from 1 to 5 is 20. What is the average value of f on [1, 5]?
a.why: The width is 5 − 1 = 4, so the average value is 20 ÷ 4 = 5. Dividing by 5, the end value, gives 4, which is a mistake: the width is b − a, not b.
a.clue: Divide the area by the width of the interval.

b.q: What is the average value of f(x) = 2x on [1, 4]?
b.why: The integral of 2x from 1 to 4 is [x²] from 1 to 4 = 16 − 1 = 15. The width is 3, so the average is 15 ÷ 3 = 5. The answer 15 is only the area, and has not been divided by the width.
b.clue: Find the integral first, then divide by 4 − 1.

problems.detail: The card says the integral 'gives the area'. That is only true when f(x) ≥ 0 on [a, b]. The average value uses the signed integral, so parts below the axis count as negative, not as area. The card should say this holds for functions above the x-axis, or use 'signed area'.

'Area under the curve divided by the width' is wrong for functions that go below the x-axis. The average value is the definite integral divided by b − a, not the area. A student could add areas as positives and get it wrong.

proposal.title: Average value of a function
card: The average value of f on [a, b] is 1/(b − a) × the definite integral of f(x) from a to b. In words: integrate, then divide by the width b − a.
When f(x) ≥ 0 on [a, b], the average value is the height of a rectangle on [a, b] with the same area as the region under the curve.

final.title: Average value of a function
card: The average value of \(f\) on \([a, b]\) is \(\frac{1}{b - a} \int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx\). In words: integrate, then divide by the width \(b - a\).
When \(f(x) \ge 0\) on \([a, b]\), the average value is the height of a rectangle on \([a, b]\) with the same area as the region under the curve.
The integral is signed: parts of the graph below the x-axis count as negative. So use the definite integral itself, not the total area.
Example: for \(f(x) = x^{2}\) on \([0, 3]\), the integral is \(\left[\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{3} = 9 - 0 = 9\). Dividing by the width \(3 - 0\) gives \(9 \div 3 = 3\).
final.remember: Find the signed integral first, then divide by the width \(b - a\).

a.q: The integral of \(f(x)\) from 1 to 5 is 20. What is the average value of \(f\) on \([1, 5]\)?
a.why: The width is \(5 - 1 = 4\), so the average value is \(20 \div 4 = 5\). Dividing by 5, the end value, gives 4, which is a mistake: the width is \(b - a\), not \(b\).
a.clue: Divide the integral by the width of the interval.

b.q: What is the average value of \(f(x) = 2x\) on \([1, 4]\)?
b.why: The integral of \(2x\) from 1 to 4 is \(\left[x^{2}\right]_{1}^{4} = 16 - 1 = 15\). The width is 3, so the average is \(15 \div 3 = 5\). The answer 15 is only the integral, and has not been divided by the width.
b.clue: Find the integral first, then divide by \(4 - 1\).
